traditions/evangelical-free-church/summa: Free churches formed by Scandinavian Pietists who left or were pushed out of Lutheran state churches. In the United States the Swedish Evangelical Free Church (1884) and Norwegian-Danish free church associations merged in 1950 to form the Evangelical Free Church of America (EFCA), known for a short Statement of Faith and for majoring on essentials. Trinity Evangelical Divinity School is its seminary.
traditions/evangelical-free-church/disti: Congregational free church from Scandinavian Pietism
traditions/evangelical-free-church/profi: Scripture as inerrant Word of God; EFCA Statement of Faith.
Salvation by grace through faith in Christ alone.
Baptism and the Lord's Supper as ordinances; both believer's and infant baptism historically tolerated.
Congregational, with a cooperative national association.
traditions/evangelical-covenant-church/s: Founded in Chicago in 1885 by Swedish immigrant Mission Friends, heirs of the Swedish Pietist revival (Carl Olof Rosenius, Paul Peter Waldenström) that formed the Mission Covenant Church of Sweden (1878). The Covenant asks 'Where is it written?' and seeks freedom in non-essentials, permitting both infant and believer's baptism.
traditions/evangelical-covenant-church/d: Pietist heritage of conversion and devotional life
'Where is it written?' — biblical question as test
Both infant and believer baptism practised
traditions/evangelical-covenant-church/p: Scripture as the only perfect rule for faith, doctrine and conduct.
Salvation by grace through faith; new life in Christ.
Baptism (infants or believers) and the Lord's Supper as sacraments.
Hope of Christ's return without a fixed millennial view.
Congregational with a connectional covenant of churches.
Evangelical worship with Scandinavian hymn heritage.
traditions/evangelical-covenant-church/s: Active; in 2023 it expelled a regional conference and churches over affirmation of same-sex relationships.
traditions/christian-and-missionary-alli: Founded in 1887 by the former Presbyterian minister A. B. Simpson in New York as two societies (Christian Alliance and Evangelical Missionary Alliance) merged in 1897. Simpson's 'Fourfold Gospel' (Christ as Saviour, Sanctifier, Healer and Coming King) shaped early Pentecostalism, though the Alliance rejected tongues as the necessary evidence of the Spirit. Its missions produced large churches in Vietnam, Indonesia, Gabon and elsewhere.
Became a denomination only gradually (1974 in USA)
Scripture as inerrant Word of God.
Salvation by grace through faith; a subsequent crisis of sanctification and ongoing Spirit-filled life.
Believers' baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper; anointing of the sick for healing.
Premillennial return of Christ as a motive for missions.
Mixed: local churches with a General Council and districts.
traditions/moravian-church/summary: The renewal of the old Unity of the Brethren (Unitas Fratrum) among refugees from Moravia on Count Nicolaus von Zinzendorf's estate at Herrnhut, Saxony, where a profound communion service on 13 August 1727 is remembered as its spiritual birthday. From 1732 Moravians pioneered Protestant world mission (Caribbean, Greenland, Suriname, South Africa) and deeply influenced John Wesley. The largest provinces today are in Tanzania.
traditions/moravian-church/distinctives/: Heart religion centred on the wounds and love of Christ
Episcopacy maintained from the old Unity
traditions/moravian-church/profile/autho: Scripture as the sole standard of doctrine; ecumenical creeds and the Augsburg Confession respected; Ground of the Unity (1957).
traditions/moravian-church/profile/salva: Salvation by grace through faith in the crucified Christ; personal relationship with the Saviour.
traditions/moravian-church/profile/sacra: Infant and believer baptism and Holy Communion; the love feast as a fellowship meal.
traditions/moravian-church/profile/escha: Hope in Christ's return; emphasis on the present reign of Christ.
traditions/moravian-church/profile/gover: Unity of autonomous provinces with synods; bishops have a pastoral and ordaining role.
traditions/moravian-church/profile/worsh: Liturgical singing, love feasts, Easter sunrise services in God's Acre.
traditions/moravian-church/status: Active; c. one million members worldwide, a majority in Africa.
traditions/african-methodist-episcopal/s: The first independent Black denomination in the United States, organised in Philadelphia in 1816 under Richard Allen after Black Methodists withdrew from St George's Methodist Episcopal Church in protest at segregation. The AME Church spread across the South after emancipation, founded Wilberforce University (1856) and established strong conferences in southern and western Africa.
traditions/african-methodist-episcopal/p: Scripture, with the Methodist Articles of Religion and AME Discipline.
Wesleyan: universal grace, justification by faith, assurance and holiness.
Baptism (including infants) and the Lord's Supper.
Classical hope of Christ's return, with strong themes of liberation.
Episcopal: bishops, annual conferences and a General Conference.
Methodist liturgy blended with Black church preaching and music.
traditions/african-methodist-episcopal/s: Active; churches in the U.S., Caribbean and Africa.
traditions/ame-zion/summary: Grew from Black Methodists who left John Street Methodist Church in New York in 1796 over discrimination, forming Zion Church and in 1821 an independent connection. Known as 'the Freedom Church', it counted Harriet Tubman, Sojourner Truth and Frederick Douglass among its members and ordained women as elders in the 1890s.
traditions/ame-zion/distinctives/1: Early ordination of women (Julia Foote, Mary Small)
traditions/ame-zion/distinctives/3: Missions in Ghana, Nigeria and Liberia
traditions/ame-zion/profile/authority: Scripture, Articles of Religion and the AME Zion Discipline.
traditions/ame-zion/profile/salvation: Wesleyan: free grace, justification by faith and holiness.
traditions/ame-zion/profile/worship: Methodist order with Black church musical tradition.
traditions/united-methodist-church/summa: Formed in Dallas in 1968 by the union of the Methodist Church (itself a 1939 reunion of northern and southern Methodism and the Methodist Protestant Church) and the Evangelical United Brethren. Long the second-largest U.S. Protestant body, it is a worldwide church with growing conferences in Africa and the Philippines. After decades of dispute over sexuality, roughly a quarter of U.S. congregations left in 2019–2023, many joining the Global Methodist Church (2022); the 2024 General Conference removed restrictions on gay clergy and same-sex weddings.
traditions/united-methodist-church/disti: Connexional polity with bishops and itinerant appointment of clergy
Social Principles and Book of Resolutions
Ordination of women (full clergy rights since 1956)
traditions/united-methodist-church/profi: Scripture as primary, interpreted with tradition, experience and reason; Articles of Religion, EUB Confession and Wesley's Sermons and Notes as doctrinal standards.
Wesleyan: prevenient, justifying and sanctifying grace; salvation open to all.
Baptism (infants and adults) and Holy Communion as sacraments; open table.
Classical hope of resurrection and new creation.
Episcopal and connexional: General, jurisdictional, central and annual conferences; bishops appoint pastors.
Liturgical and free forms; Wesley hymns; the United Methodist Hymnal.
traditions/united-methodist-church/statu: Active; reshaped by the 2019–2024 disaffiliations and regionalisation.
traditions/free-methodist-church/summary: Organised at Pekin, New York, in 1860 after B. T. Roberts and others were expelled from the Methodist Episcopal Church for preaching a stricter holiness. It stood for free pews for the poor, opposition to slavery and secret societies, and entire sanctification. Now a worldwide holiness denomination.
traditions/free-methodist-church/distinc: Early support for women in ministry
traditions/free-methodist-church/profile: Scripture with the Free Methodist Articles of Religion.
Wesleyan-Arminian with entire sanctification as a second work of grace.
Return of Christ and final judgment.
traditions/free-methodist-church/status: Active; worldwide membership mostly outside North America.
traditions/wesleyan-church/summary: Formed in 1968 by the merger of the Wesleyan Methodist Church, founded in 1843 by abolitionists leaving the Methodist Episcopal Church, and the Pilgrim Holiness Church (1897). Its seminary and universities (Indiana Wesleyan, Houghton) make it a significant voice of Wesleyan-Holiness evangelicalism.
traditions/wesleyan-church/distinctives/: Ordination of women since its origins
traditions/wesleyan-church/profile/autho: Scripture as inerrant, with the Wesleyan Articles of Religion.
traditions/wesleyan-church/profile/gover: Conference-based with a General Conference and general superintendents.
traditions/church-of-the-nazarene/summar: The largest Wesleyan-Holiness denomination, formed by the union of regional holiness churches culminating at Pilot Point, Texas, in 1908. Founders included Phineas F. Bresee of Los Angeles. It teaches entire sanctification as a second definite work of grace and has a strong international presence, with a majority of members outside the United States.
traditions/church-of-the-nazarene/distin: Women in ministry from the beginning
Rejection of tongues as initial evidence
traditions/church-of-the-nazarene/profil: Scripture as inerrantly revealing God's will in matters of salvation; Articles of Faith in the Manual.
Wesleyan-Arminian: justification by faith, followed by entire sanctification cleansing the heart from original sin.
Baptism (infants or believers; any mode) and the Lord's Supper.
Premillennial return not required; Christ's return, resurrection and judgment.
Mixed episcopal-congregational: districts, district superintendents and general superintendents; General Assembly.
traditions/church-of-the-nazarene/status: Active; self-reports about 2.6 million members worldwide.
traditions/church-of-god-anderson/summar: A holiness reformation movement begun by Daniel S. Warner in 1881, rejecting denominational structures as man-made divisions and calling Christians 'out of Babylon' into the visible unity of the one church of God. Headquartered in Anderson, Indiana, it remains non-Pentecostal and treats membership as conversion rather than enrolment.
traditions/church-of-god-anderson/profil: Wesleyan holiness: new birth and sanctification.
Believers' baptism by immersion, the Lord's Supper and feet washing.
Amillennial, historically reading Revelation as church history.
